 Mayor-elect Raman faces scrutiny from the left and the right 
 By Chris Woodward | The Center Square contributor

 (The Center Square) - Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman is pivoting from a contentious election battle to a message of unity at City Hall, though political observers warn the Democratic Socialist faces immediate scrutiny over her past voting record and unanswered policy questions on homelessness and public safety.
 Liberals and conservatives alike are watching Raman during the weeks leading up to her being sworn-in on Dec. 14.
 Raman, a Los Angeles City Council member for District 4, defeated Mayor Karen Bass in the Nov. 3 general election, campaigning as an anti-establishment reformer. 
 The victory followed a sharp ideological clash between the two Democratic candidates. During their final debate in October, Bass questioned Raman’s readiness to govern a city of 3.8 million people, pointing to a lack of endorsements from fellow council members and accusing Raman of having a problem with constituents. Raman rejected the accusation as a "lie" and criticized Bass for years of decline, mismanagement and excuses.
 The two also divided sharply over local policing ahead of the 2028 Olympics. While Bass emphasized police staffing and leadership stability, Raman criticized Los Angeles Police Department pay raises and pledged to work with the Police Commission to replace Police Chief Jim McDonnell.
 Since the election, Raman has sought to lower the political temperature. In a Nov. 5 video statement posted on X, the mayor-elect thanked her grassroots supporters and paid tribute to Bass’ decades of public service as an emergency room nurse, community organizer, state legislator, member of Congress and the city’s first female mayor. Bass is a former California Assembly speaker
 The Center Square reached out to Raman for an interview, but did not hear back in time for this story.
 Progressive organizers say Raman's win on Nov. 3 represents a clear mandate from voters tired of the status quo. Joshua Gleason, co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America – Long Beach chapter, which covers parts of Los Angeles including San Pedro and the South Bay, told The Center Square that the election reflects a desire for change from the Democrats and Republicans who have long held power in the city.
 "We are happy to have someone with a history in DSA in LA's highest executive office," Gleason said. He added his chapter plans to work alongside the DSA - Los Angeles chapter to push her to deliver for working-class Angelenos rather than corporations and special interests.
 Gleason pointed to housing and affordability as the most urgent issues awaiting Raman, highlighting her pledges to establish an office of tenant protections, tighten rules on illegal short-term rentals, audit homelessness spending and cut street encampments by 50% by the end of 2028. He noted Raman's proposed tenant protections office could work in tandem with newly elected City Attorney Marissa Roy, also a DSA member, to enforce housing policies and provide legal representation for renters.
 Gleason added his chapter is watching closely to ensure Raman follows through on her commitment to work with the Police Commission to replace Chief McDonnell. He cited reports of LAPD data going to federal immigration authorities and police officers providing crowd control during U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests, saying the department's denials of cooperation with ICE have failed to reassure immigrant communities.
 Despite the post-election outreach and progressive backing, critics argue Raman will be judged on concrete results rather than campaign rhetoric, particularly on fiscal and regulatory issues affecting taxpayers and neighboring communities.
 Republican strategist and former Spencer Pratt campaign staffer Gus Portela said that while voters were clearly looking for "fresh blood," Raman enters office with major vulnerabilities regarding her judgment and credibility. Pratt lost to Raman and Bass in the Los Angeles primary on June 2.
 "She backed a housing tax and later acknowledged the damage on housing construction, and to this day, Angelenos haven't gotten an answer on that," Portela told The Center Square about Raman. "In public safety, she needs to reconcile essentially her voting record with her promises. She also needs to own her share of City Hall's failures and ensure that she's being fully transparent."
 According to Portela, Raman must quickly clarify how her administration will differ from Bass’ on key operational fronts, including construction of homeless shelters and whether she will use law enforcement to prevent new homeless encampments.
 "There's a lot of things that she's yet to answer as a mayoral candidate, and now that she's mayor, she needs to answer,” Portela said.
 Both Portela and Gleason emphasized that Los Angeles' policy choices on housing, homelessness and crime carry regional consequences across Southern California.
 Portela warned that mismanagement in Los Angeles directly impacts surrounding suburbs and that labor unions and critics alike will be "holding her feet to the fire."
 Gleason noted cities across Los Angeles County — including Long Beach, the county's second-largest city — are deeply interdependent, as housing shortages in Los Angeles can drive displacement into neighboring municipalities.
 Bass heads into office, knowing that the top elected officials of the city and county of Los Angeles backed Bass.
 Four of the five Los Angeles County supervisors endorsed Bass for reelection: Hilda Solis (District 1), Holly Mitchell (District 2), Janice Hahn (District 4), and Kathryn Barger (District 5). Lindsey Horvath (District 3) – who just recently announced a 2028 campaign for Los Angeles County CEO, which is becoming an elected position – was the only supervisor who backed Raman.
 Many of the City Council members  endorsed Bass for reelection. Among them are Council President Marqueece Harris-Dawson (District 8), Eunisses Hernandez (District 1), Ysabel Jurado (District 14), Hugo Soto-Martinez (District 13), Katy Yaroslavsky (District 5), Curren Price (District 9), Imelda Padilla (District 6), Monica Rodriguez (District 7) and John Lee (District 12).
 On Nov. 10, Raman  addressed the Los Angeles City Council, praising individual members across the political spectrum for their work on issues ranging from unarmed crisis response and small business support to port operations and public safety.
 "In me, you will have something that not every mayor has [been]: a partner who understands what it means to be a council member," Raman told her colleagues.
 The Center Square’s requests for comments from city council members, Los Angeles County supervisors and DSA-Los Angeles did not receive a response.
